pr_body:
The new location expansion pattern `rlocationpath` and its plural version `rlocationpaths` resolve to the path(s) suitable for the Rlocation function offered by runfiles libraries.

Compared to the `rootpath` pattern, which can returns `../repo_name/pkg/file` for a file in an external repository and `pkg/file` for a file in the main repository, the path returned by `rlocationpath` is always of the form `repo_name/pkg/file`.

RELNOTES: The new path variable `$(rlocationpath ...)` and its plural form `$(rlocationpaths ...)` can be used to expand labels to the paths accepted by the `Rlocation` function of runfiles libraries. This is the preferred way to access data dependencies at runtime and works on all platforms, even when runfiles are not enabled (e.g., on Windows by default).

Work towards #16124
Fixes #10923
pr_comments:
@lberki Can you review this (or delegate to someone else)?

I haven't included any changes to docs yet, but could add them if the rest of the PR looks good. There are no docs on runfiles libraries yet though, so whatever I include in this PR will still be lacking context.

Also note, the name might cause some confusion when bash's `$()` is used. If you're doing substitutions you'll need something like `$$(rlocation $(rlocation //label))` where inner one is substituted and `$$` is unescaped.

> If I understand correctly, please confirm, rlocation always needs `repo_name/path/in/the/repo` as input.
Exactly.

> And this can be `_main/path/in/the/main/repo`. Right? 

Yes, for all files in the main repo, with Bzlmod enabled. Without Bzlmod, this would be `__main__/path` or `<workspace name>/path` (if a name is set).

> What happens in the case this is a generated file - that is in `bazel-bin/reponame/...`?

Both generated and source file's use the same `repo/package/path/in/repo/name` path structure, just like in the runfiles directory.

> Possible alternative would be `$(reponame @repo//label)`, but this worse since you'd need to use 2 functions.

It's also difficult to get the remaining part since `rootpath` for an external repository doesn't just return `package/path/in/repo/name`, AFAIK it returns `../repo/package/path/in/repo/name`.

> About the name. `location(s)` function is deprecated. I'm guessing you chose the name so it fits `rlocation` function (for example the one here https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/blob/master/tools/bash/runfiles/runfiles.bash). So this then looks like `rlocation $(rlocation //label)`.

I chose `rlocationpath` instead of `rlocation` for two reasons: 

1. To prevent confusing this with the deprecated `location` function, making it more similar to the recommended `{exec,root}path` functions.
2. To distinguish it from the `rlocation` functions defined by runfiles libraries, which are supposed to take whatever `$(rlocationpath //label)` evaluates to.

Your example would be `rlocation $1` with `args = ["$(rlocationpath //label)"]`. 

> Does the plural form make sense here?

I think so, yes. In Java, it would be easy to do `Arrays.stream(args).map(arg -> r.rlocation(arg))`, making use of the implicit shell tokenization of the `args` attribute.


> Because of deprecation of `location`, perhaps consider another name, like `repopath`? Maybe `rlocation $(repopath //label)` looks better?

See above, do you think `rlocationpath` does a sufficient job at preventing this confusion? This expansion has one very clear purpose, providing the correct path for the `rlocation` function, so I think that `rlocation` should be in the name - otherwise it will be very hard to distinguish `execpath` and `rootpath` from the new expansion.

> 
> Slightly out of scope, but do you think there's a way to simplify copy-pasted lines we have in almost all shell tests https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/blob/master/src/test/shell/bazel/archive_contents_test.sh#L20-L40 or https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/blob/master/src/test/shell/bazel/android/android_helper.sh#L17-L26?

The latter one is more modern and already quite a bit shorter. I don't see a way to fundamentally improve on that.

> One more naive question. Can we provide a function that directly returns what rlocation $(rlocation //label) would return? Eliminating the need for first/external rlocation.

> Also note, the name might cause some confusion when bash's $() is used. If you're doing substitutions you'll need something like $$(rlocation $(rlocation //label)) where inner one is substituted and $$ is unescaped.

Answering these in one as they are related: You wouldn't commonly do this since `$(rlocationpath //label)` has to be evaluated by Bazel, whereas `$(rlocation repo/some/path)` is an actual Bash function call happening at runtime. 

We *could* think about ways to make `$(rlocation //label)` work from Bash directly, but that would require major changes to the runfiles tree - essentially, we would need to dump an additional manifest file that lists the contents of `DefaultInfo.files` for all Bazel targets contributing runfiles to a given executable. @lberki who has been interested in improving the usability of runfiles in this direction.

Hello @comius, Above PR is awaiting to merge. What should be done for the internal fixes which we discussed offline, Can you please have a look. Thanks!

> Hey I had one more thought. Is it possible to put this function under an experimental flag or only enable together with bzlmod? 

Could you explain why you think this is a risky feature to add unconditionally? The paths it returns are tied to a stable, in-use feature, the runfiles libraries. If we introduce a new way to access runfiles in the future and deprecate the libraries, we will have to offer a migration plan for users anyway. Whether we have `$(rlocationpath ..)` around as a stable feature shouldn't affect that migration since it doesn't do anything by itself - we could just make it undocumented and phase it out together with the libraries. Do you see any additional maintenance burden in this new location expansion?

I am asking because guarding this feature behind a flag would make rulesets essentially unable to rely on it. Since `--enable_blzmod` has other effects, we would need a separate flag. In fact, the main use case of this feature would be for existing `WORKSPACE` projects, where the workspace runfiles directory name isn't fixed and thus not easy to obtain from a macro (see https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/10923).

> What I'm worried is that direction on how to fix runfiles might still change - considering there are new bugs showing up.

Which new bugs are you referring to? We still have the ongoing discussion in https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/15029, but I am not aware of any bugs.

If we introduce a new way to access runfiles in the future and deprecate the libraries, we will have to offer a migration plan for users anyway. Whether we have `$(rlocationpath ..)` around as a stable feature shouldn't affect that migration since it doesn't do anything by itself - we could just make it undocumented and phase it out together with the libraries. Do you see any additional maintenance burden in this new location expansion?

We should consider adding any new features risky. We often didn't do that, arguing the new feature is completely foolproof. For example rule.name. This sometimes resulted in a lot of effort to do a cleanup. The users should be aware this is new and we should have some incubation period to derisk.

I was referring to https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/16379.

@comius I am definitely _not_ convinced that the current approach to runfiles discovery is optimal and do think that more fundamental changes to this mechanism aren't unlikely. I greatly value your caution when it comes to proposed API changes!

I do think that the _incremental_ risk of adding `$(rlocationpath ...)` is very low though: It is only useful in conjunction with the current approach to runfiles (but in that case, it is very useful), so it would live and die with that without causing additional migration efforts. The code introduced in this PR is also not very complex, I would argue that the switch to an enum even makes the existing code more readable.

I actually think that this PR could simplify potential future migrations as using `$(rlocationpath ...)` sidesteps the entire "repo mapping manifest applied to hardcoded runfiles paths" thing and instead emits a path under our control that could be changed transparently in future releases (we could add a note to the docs stating clearly that the precise nature of the returned path is not defined, but instead is whatever `Rlocation` accepts).

What do you think? If you still aren't convinced, I would introduce this behind an `--experimental_enable_rlocationpath` flag.

issue_context.title: Get the name of current repository from macro
issue_context.body:
### Description of the problem / feature request:
I am trying to get the name of the current repository from a macro.
```
.
├── a
│   ├── BUILD.bazel
│   ├── WORKSPACE
│   ├── empty.txt
│   └── txt_files.bzl
└── b
    ├── BUILD.bazel
    ├── WORKSPACE
    └── empty2.txt
```
_(see full example [here](https://github.com/or-shachar/bazel_repository_name_issue) )_

I want that if repo `b` will call the macro in `@a//:txt_files.bzl` then somehow I'd be able to retrieve that it was called from repo `b`.

Right now (not sure if it's a bug or work as intended) - calling `native.repository_name()` will return `@` and not the name of repo as declared in its `WORKSPACE` file.

### Feature requests: what underlying problem are you trying to solve with this feature?

I want to change the behavior of a macro based on the callee repository.

Can we allow `native.repository_name()` to return the explicit name of the repository and not `@`?  To maintain backward compatibility - I assume it would be better if we add a flag to this method that will be turned off by default.
comments:
As a workaround I wrote the following repository rule:
```python
def _define_repository_name_impl(repository_ctx):
    repository_ctx.file("BUILD.bazel",
        """package(default_visibility = ["//visibility:public"])
        """)
    repository_ctx.file("defs.bzl",
        """main_repository_name="{}"
        """.format(repository_ctx.attr.repo_name))

_define_repository_name = repository_rule(
    implementation = _define_repository_name_impl,
    attrs={"repo_name": attr.string(mandatory=True)}
  )

def define_repository_name(repo_name):
    _define_repository_name(name = "main_repository_name",repo_name = repo_name)

```

which allows me to load the main repository name by calling:
```python
load("@main_repository_name//:defs.bzl","main_repository_name")
```

The `WORKSPACE` file looks like this:
```python
repository_name = "xxx"
workspace(name = repository_name)

load("@bazel_tooling//rules:define_repository_name.bzl","define_repository_name")
define_repository_name(repository_name)
```

I don't like it... given that `workspace()` call should be the first line of the WORKSPACE file. But it works (`bazel 2.1.0`)
hey @laurentlb ... May I ask for your opinion on this matter? :-)
@or-shachar I have the same issue, did you ever find a resolution to this?

@or-shachar @jheaff1 Could you describe in more detail what you want to use the name declared in the `WORKSPACE` file for in a macro? Knowing more about the actual problem you are trying to solve would help me answer these questions.

You most likely want just "@" instead. With the recent fixes on repo mapping, "@workspace_name//:foo" is equivalent to "@//:foo".

(Unless you're doing exec path or runfiles shenanigans, in which case refer to @fmeum's comment.)

@fmeum I am trying to write a sh_binary target for the rules_foreign_cc repo that wraps around an executable binary (built by rules_foreign_cc) with shared library dependencies. This would allow such a binary to be used as a build tool, eg the protobuf compiler or various generators part of the Qt framework.

I would like to use the `rlocation` bash function provided here:

https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/blob/a76cf2f4c3aa514dffa1ddc038c196103ae4583c/tools/bash/runfiles/runfiles.bash#L68

The `rlocation` bash function requires the workspace name, which I would like to obtain programatically in a macro.

I’ve tried to use native.repository_name() but that returns `@` rather than the name of the repository.

@jheaff1 Would an analogue of `$(location //foo)` that returns the correct path for `rlocation` help you realize this? I could see that being more user-friendly than yet another "some type of name of a repo" thing.
@fmeum Absolutely that would be very useful. Ive found that using `$(rootpath` rather than `$(location` provides exactly what `$(rlocation` requires apart from the workspace name.

@lberki I have been thinking about proposing a `$(location ...)` variant that returns the correct path for Rlocation for a while. The way runfiles work with Bzlmod would almost make this a requirement for location expansion to remain useful in `args`. What do you think?

@fmeum without taking sides on the `$(location) question, it's a feature orthogonal to the one proposed in this bug.

re: this bug in particular, what is the argument *against* introducing `repository_name()`? Naively, one would think that it's a very logical extension to `package_name()`. @Wyverald maybe you can think of a counter-argument?

> this bug in particular, what is the argument against introducing repository_name()? Naively, one would think that it's a very logical extension to package_name(). @Wyverald maybe you can think of a counter-argument?

We already have `native.repository_name` and it does what it says on the tin (https://bazel.build/rules/lib/native#repository_name). @fmeum's & @jheaff1's question is more about the runfiles/execpath use case, where we sometimes need the *workspace name*, which is only accessible right now in a rule ctx object (https://bazel.build/rules/lib/ctx#workspace_name; also to note, *not* the same as [Label.workspace_name](https://bazel.build/rules/lib/Label#workspace_name)...)
@Wyverald I'm embarrassed! I specifically looked for the identifier called `repository_name` and didn't find it in the source code. My bad.

The issue with making the (global) workspace name available in Starlark code is that then the evaluation of BUILD files in external repositories would be a function of the content of the main repository, which isn't too intuitive (it's problematic enough for `ctx.workspace_name()`, but we can't help that because that's how runfiles work at the moment.

@lberki That plus the fact that having yet another `workspace_name` would be confusing made me think that being able to get Rlocation paths out of location expansion may indeed be the best solution to this issue (see also the comment by @jheaff1). Since `native.repository_name` returns the right identifier for everything *except* runfiles discovery, why not add a way for users to get the full runfiles path right away without having them stitch it together themselves?

The reason why I was confused is that for some reason, I thought `$(rlocation)` is already a thing in Bazel so I went on a wild goose chase trying to figure out what *else* you want :)

I think both adding `$(rlocation)` and the same method to File is reasonable. @Wyverald , it looks like you also agree?

@lberki `$(rlocation)` seems reasonably easy to do, but `File.rlocation_path` is difficult: Without `--experimental_sibling_repository_layout`, that function needs to know the workspace name. I'm not sure how the API for that would look like, should we just let the user pass in `ctx`?

Not necessarily; there is `BazelStarlarkContext`, which is available to the Java implementations of Starlark functions without an extra argument and it, weirdly, already contains the repository name of the tools repository. So I could imagine plumbing the workspace name in there that way, too. Rule implementations need to know the name of the main workspace anyway, so it would probably not require too much extra plumbing.
@lberki I will give that a try. We will have to make a concession though: Using `StarlarkThread` is incompatible with `structField = True`, so this will have to be a function instead.

Today I Learned. It seems to be an artificial choice and not an inherent limitation of how Starlark works, though, and I don't see an immediate reason for this limitation. @c-parsons , do you remember why you prohibited setting `useStarlarkThread` and `structField` to true at the same time in 73e1016 ?
